q: A café offers 4 kinds of bread, 3 fillings and 2 sauces. A sandwich uses exactly one bread, one filling and one sauce. How many different sandwiches are possible?
x: Each choice is made in turn, so by the multiplication principle there are 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 sandwiches. Adding the choices (4 + 3 + 2 = 9) would count picking one item from any group, not one from each group.

q: How many three-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if no digit may be repeated?
x: There are 5 choices for the hundreds digit, then 4 for the tens and 3 for the units: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. 125 = 5³ allows repetition, and 10 = C(5, 3) only chooses the digits without arranging them.

q: Let C(n, r) be the number of ways to choose r objects from n different objects. What is the value of C(8, 3) + C(8, 4)?
x: C(8, 3) = 56 and C(8, 4) = 70, so the sum is 126; this agrees with Pascal's rule C(8, 3) + C(8, 4) = C(9, 4) = 126. Choosing 84 = C(9, 3) uses the wrong lower index in Pascal's rule.

q: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability that the number shown is a prime number?
x: The primes among 1 to 6 are 2, 3 and 5, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2. Counting 1 as a prime gives the wrong value 4/6 = 2/3; 1 is not prime.

q: A lock code has 3 characters, and each character is one of the digits 0 to 9. Digits may be repeated. How many different codes are possible?
x: Each of the 3 positions has 10 choices, so there are 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 codes (000 to 999). 720 = 10 × 9 × 8 wrongly forbids repetition, and 999 forgets the code 000.

q: Six people, including Ahmed and Bilal, stand in a row. In how many arrangements do Ahmed and Bilal stand next to each other?
x: Treat Ahmed and Bilal as one block: the block and the other 4 people give 5 units, arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Inside the block the two can swap, so the total is 2 × 120 = 240. Answering 120 forgets the internal order of the pair.

q: A class of 10 students must choose 2 representatives with equal roles. In how many ways can this be done?
x: The order does not matter, so the number is C(10, 2) = (10 × 9)/2 = 45. The value 90 = 10 × 9 counts each pair twice, as if the two roles were different.

q: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 3 green balls of the same size. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is blue or green?
x: There are 3 + 3 = 6 blue or green balls out of 10, so the probability is 6/10 = 3/5. The value 2/5 is the probability of red, the complement.

q: A restaurant menu has 3 starters and 5 main courses. A meal is one starter and one main course. How many different meals are possible?
x: By the multiplication principle there are 3 × 5 = 15 meals. Adding 3 + 5 = 8 would count choosing one dish only, and 30 counts each meal twice.

q: Six people, including Amina and Carlos, stand in a row. In how many arrangements are Amina and Carlos NOT next to each other?
x: All arrangements: 6! = 720. Arrangements with the two together: 2 × 5! = 240. So the number with them apart is 720 − 240 = 480. The option 240 is the number of arrangements where they are together.

q: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can the committee contain exactly 2 boys?
x: Choose 2 of the 5 boys and 1 of the 4 girls: C(5, 2) × C(4, 1) = 10 × 4 = 40. 84 = C(9, 3) is the number of all committees, with no condition on the boys.

q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 8?
x: Among 36 equally likely ordered outcomes, sum 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2): 5 outcomes, so 5/36. Counting only unordered pairs {2,6}, {3,5}, {4,4} gives 3/36 = 1/12, but those pairs are not equally likely.

q: How many positive divisors does 72 have?
x: 72 = 2³ × 3², and each divisor is 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ with a ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} and b ∈ {0, 1, 2}, so there are 4 × 3 = 12 divisors. Multiplying the exponents (3 × 2 = 6) forgets the choice of exponent 0.

q: How many different arrangements of the letters of the word BANANA are there?
x: BANANA has 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N repeated 2 times, so the count is 6!/(3! × 2!) = 720/12 = 60. 120 = 6!/3! only allows for the repeated A's and forgets the two N's.

q: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can the committee contain at least one girl?
x: Use the complement: all committees C(9, 3) = 84 minus all-boy committees C(5, 3) = 10 gives 74. Subtracting the all-girl committees C(4, 3) = 4 instead gives the wrong value 80.

q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 10?
x: Sum 10: 3 outcomes, sum 11: 2 outcomes, sum 12: 1 outcome, total 6 of 36, so 6/36 = 1/6. The value 1/12 = 3/36 counts only sums 11 and 12, forgetting the sum 10.

q: Using the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with no digit repeated, how many four-digit even numbers can be formed?
x: Last digit 0: the other three places take 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 ways. Last digit 2 or 4: the first digit cannot be 0 or the last digit, so 4 choices, then 4 × 3 for the middle: 2 × 48 = 96. Total 60 + 96 = 156. The value 96 forgets the numbers ending in 0, and 180 ignores that 0 cannot lead.

q: How many diagonals does a convex octagon (8 sides) have?
x: Any 2 of the 8 vertices give C(8, 2) = 28 segments; 8 of these are sides, so there are 28 − 8 = 20 diagonals. 28 forgets to remove the sides.

q: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
x: There are 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes, and exactly 2 heads occurs in HHT, HTH, THH: 3 outcomes, so 3/8. The value 1/4 wrongly treats the 4 possible numbers of heads (0, 1, 2, 3) as equally likely.

q: Five students stand in a line. Carlos must not stand at either end. How many arrangements are possible?
x: Carlos takes one of the 3 middle places, and the other 4 students fill the rest in 4! = 24 ways: 3 × 24 = 72. Equivalently 120 − 2 × 24 = 72. The value 96 = 120 − 24 removes only one end.

q: There are 10 points in a plane. Exactly 4 of them lie on one straight line, and no other three points are collinear. How many triangles have all three vertices among these points?
x: Any 3 points give C(10, 3) = 120 choices, but the C(4, 3) = 4 choices taken from the collinear points give no triangle. So there are 120 − 4 = 116 triangles. The value 120 forgets the collinear points.

q: Two cards are drawn at the same time from six cards numbered 1 to 6. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even?
x: The product is odd only if both cards are odd: C(3, 2) = 3 of C(6, 2) = 15 pairs. So P(even) = 1 − 3/15 = 4/5. The value 1/5 is the probability of an odd product.

q: In how many ways can 4 different flags be hung in a row on a pole?
x: There are 4 choices for the first place, 3 for the second, 2 for the third and 1 for the last: 4! = 24. The value 256 = 4⁴ allows the same flag to be used more than once.

q: A shelf holds 5 different mathematics books, 4 different physics books and 3 different chemistry books. In how many ways can Kwame choose 2 books from different subjects?
x: Add the three subject pairs: maths–physics 5 × 4 = 20, maths–chemistry 5 × 3 = 15, physics–chemistry 4 × 3 = 12, total 47. The value 66 = C(12, 2) also includes pairs from the same subject.

q: Three boys and two girls stand in a row in random order. What is the probability that the two girls stand at the two ends?
x: The girls occupy 2 of the 5 places, and all C(5, 2) = 10 pairs of places are equally likely; only one pair is the two ends, so the probability is 1/10. Equivalently 2! × 3!/5! = 12/120. The value 2/5 is only the probability that one particular girl stands at an end.

q: Eight runners take part in a race. In how many ways can the gold and silver medals be awarded (no ties)?
x: Gold can go to any of 8 runners and silver to any of the remaining 7, so there are 8 × 7 = 56 ways. The value 28 = C(8, 2) ignores that gold and silver are different medals.

q: Six different books are shared among three students, Ahmed, Amina and Kwame, so that each student gets exactly 2 books. In how many ways can this be done?
x: Ahmed's 2 books can be chosen in C(6, 2) = 15 ways, Amina's in C(4, 2) = 6 ways and Kwame takes the last 2: 15 × 6 = 90. The value 15 = 90/3! counts only the splits into three unnamed pairs, but here the students are different.

q: An integer is chosen at random from 1 to 20. What is the probability that it is divisible by 3 or by 5?
x: Multiples of 3: 6 numbers; multiples of 5: 4 numbers; 15 is in both lists. So 6 + 4 − 1 = 9 numbers and the probability is 9/20. Adding 6 + 4 = 10 to get 1/2 counts 15 twice.

q: In how many ways can 5 people sit around a round table, if only their positions relative to each other matter?
x: Fix one person's seat to remove rotations; the other 4 people can then be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. The value 120 = 5! counts each seating 5 times, once for each rotation.

q: A team of 4 is chosen from 6 men and 5 women. In how many ways can the team have exactly 2 men and 2 women?
x: Choose the men in C(6, 2) = 15 ways and the women in C(5, 2) = 10 ways; multiply: 15 × 10 = 150. Adding 15 + 10 = 25 is wrong because each choice of men goes with every choice of women, and 330 = C(11, 4) ignores the condition.

q: Which of the following values can be the probability of an event?
x: Any probability P satisfies 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, and only 0.75 lies in this interval. A negative value such as −0.2 and values above 1 such as 4/3 and 1.05 are impossible.

q: Four-digit numbers are formed using each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 exactly once. How many of them are greater than 2300?
x: First digit 3 or 4: 2 × 3! = 12 numbers. First digit 2: the second digit must be 3 or 4, giving 2 × 2! = 4 numbers (2314, 2341, 2413, 2431). Total 16. The value 12 forgets the numbers beginning with 2.

q: The probability that event A happens is 0.35. What is the probability that A does not happen?
x: Complementary events have probabilities adding to 1, so P(not A) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. The value 1.35 adds instead of subtracting and is greater than 1, which is impossible.

q: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A ∪ B), the probability that at least one of them happens?
x: Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. The value 0.9 simply adds the probabilities, which is only correct for mutually exclusive events.

q: Three players shoot at a target independently. Their probabilities of hitting it are 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. What is the probability that the target is hit at least once?
x: All three miss with probability (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1/4, so at least one hit has probability 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The value 1/4 is the probability that everyone misses, and 1/24 is the probability that all three hit.

q: What is the value of 7!/5!?
x: 7!/5! = 7 × 6 × 5!/5! = 7 × 6 = 42. 210 = 7 × 6 × 5 cancels one factor too few, and 2 comes from dividing 7 − 5 as if factorials cancelled like numbers.

q: For n ≥ 2, which expression equals n! − (n − 1)!?
What is the units digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50!?
x: From 5! onwards every factorial contains 2 × 5, so it ends in 0. The units digit therefore comes from 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33, which is 3. Choosing 0 forgets the first four terms.

q: How many four-digit numbers have all four digits even?
x: The even digits are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. The first digit cannot be 0 (4 choices), and each of the other three has 5 choices: 4 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 500. 625 = 5⁴ wrongly allows a leading 0.

q: Zara can travel from Lahore to Islamabad by any one of 4 trains or 6 buses. In how many ways can she go and come back if she returns by a different vehicle from the one she went by?
x: By the addition principle she has 4 + 6 = 10 ways to go; any of the other 9 vehicles can bring her back, so 10 × 9 = 90 ways. 100 allows the same vehicle both ways, and 48 multiplies 4 × 6 × 2 instead of adding.

q: A quiz has 5 multiple-choice questions, each with 4 options and exactly one correct option. In how many ways can a student answer every question and get all of them wrong?
x: Each question has 3 wrong options, and the choices are independent, so 3⁵ = 243. 1024 = 4⁵ counts all possible answer sheets; 15 adds 3 five times instead of multiplying.

q: How many three-digit numbers contain the digit 7 at least once?
x: There are 900 three-digit numbers. Those with no 7: first digit 8 choices (1–9 except 7), the others 9 each, giving 8 × 9 × 9 = 648. So 900 − 648 = 252 contain a 7. 648 is the complement itself.

q: How many even three-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 if digits may be repeated?
x: The units digit must be 2, 4 or 6 (3 choices), and the hundreds and tens digits have 6 choices each: 6 × 6 × 3 = 108. 216 = 6³ ignores the even condition, and 60 forbids repetition.

q: Which expression equals the product 2 × 4 × 6 × … × 20?
x: Take a factor 2 out of each of the 10 terms: 2 × 4 × … × 20 = 2¹⁰ × (1 × 2 × … × 10) = 2¹⁰ × 10!. Taking out only one 2 gives 2 × 10!, and 20!/10! is 11 × 12 × … × 20.

q: Which expression equals the product of the first n odd numbers, 1 × 3 × 5 × … × (2n − 1)?
x: (2n)! is the product of the odd numbers times the even numbers 2 × 4 × … × 2n = 2ⁿ × n!. Dividing gives (2n)!/(2ⁿ × n!). Check n = 3: 720/(8 × 6) = 15 = 1 × 3 × 5.

q: In how many ways can 4 different letters be posted in 3 different letter boxes, if any box may receive any number of letters?
x: Each letter independently goes into one of 3 boxes, so 3⁴ = 81. 64 = 4³ reverses the roles (each box choosing a letter), and 12 = 4 × 3 multiplies instead of using powers.

q: A number plate has 3 different letters from A to Z followed by 3 digits, which may repeat. How many plates are possible?
x: Letters: 26 × 25 × 24 = 15,600; digits: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000; total 15,600 × 1000 = 15,600,000. 17,576,000 lets the letters repeat, and 11,232,000 forbids the digits to repeat (15,600 × 720).

q: Usman must choose exactly one optional subject, either one of 3 science subjects or one of 4 arts subjects. In how many ways can he choose?
x: He chooses from one group or the other, not both, so the addition principle gives 3 + 4 = 7. Multiplying to 12 would count choosing one science and one arts subject together.

q: How many positive integers less than 1000 can be written using only the digits 1, 2 and 3 (digits may repeat)?
x: One-digit: 3; two-digit: 3² = 9; three-digit: 3³ = 27. Adding gives 3 + 9 + 27 = 39. Counting only the three-digit numbers gives 27.

q: If P(n, 4) = 20 × P(n, 2), what is the value of n?
How many different arrangements can be made of all the letters of the word PAKISTAN?
x: PAKISTAN has 8 letters with A appearing twice, so the count is 8!/2! = 40320/2 = 20160. 40320 treats the two A's as different, and 10080 divides by an extra 2.

q: The letters of the word LAHORE are arranged so that the three vowels A, O, E are always together. How many arrangements are possible?
x: Treat A, O, E as one block: the block and L, H, R give 4 units, arranged in 4! = 24 ways, and the vowels inside the block in 3! = 6 ways: 24 × 6 = 144. Forgetting the arrangement inside the block gives 24.

q: Seven people, including Ali and Sara, sit around a round table. In how many arrangements do Ali and Sara sit next to each other?
x: Tie Ali and Sara together as one unit: 6 units around a table give (6 − 1)! = 120 arrangements, and the pair can swap seats: 120 × 2 = 240. Forgetting the swap gives 120; using 6! for a circle gives 1440.

q: In how many ways can 8 different beads be strung on a necklace, if a necklace turned over counts as the same?
x: Circular arrangements of 8 objects: (8 − 1)! = 5040. A necklace can be flipped, so clockwise and anticlockwise orders are the same: 5040/2 = 2520. 5040 is the round-table answer without the flip.

q: 5 boys and 3 girls stand in a row. In how many arrangements are no two girls next to each other?
x: Arrange the boys in 5! = 120 ways; this leaves 6 gaps (ends included), and the 3 girls take 3 different gaps in P(6, 3) = 120 ways: 120 × 120 = 14400. 4320 = 6! × 3! counts the girls all together, which is a different condition.

q: 4 different flags are available. A signal is made by hoisting one or more of them, one above the other. How many different signals can be made?
x: Order matters, so count by the number of flags: P(4, 1) + P(4, 2) + P(4, 3) + P(4, 4) = 4 + 12 + 24 + 24 = 64. Using only all 4 flags gives 24.

q: What is the value of P(8, 3)?
x: P(8, 3) = 8!/5! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. 56 is C(8, 3), which divides by 3! more, and 512 = 8³ allows repetition.

q: If C(n, 8) = C(n, 12), what is the value of C(n, 18)?
x: C(n, r) = C(n, s) with r ≠ s means r + s = n, so n = 20. Then C(20, 18) = C(20, 2) = 20 × 19/2 = 190. 380 is P(20, 2), which forgets to divide by 2.

q: At a party, every guest shook hands exactly once with every other guest, and there were 66 handshakes in all. How many guests were there?
x: Each handshake is a pair of guests, so C(n, 2) = n(n − 1)/2 = 66, giving n(n − 1) = 132 = 12 × 11 and n = 12. Using n(n − 1) = 66 would give no whole number; 11 picks the wrong factor.

q: How many three-digit numbers have their digits in strictly increasing order from left to right (for example 137)?
x: Any 3 different digits can be written in increasing order in exactly one way, and 0 can never appear (it would have to come first). So the count is C(9, 3) = 84. C(10, 3) = 120 wrongly allows 0, and 504 = P(9, 3) counts all orders.

q: A convex polygon has 35 diagonals. How many sides does it have?
x: An n-gon has C(n, 2) − n = n(n − 3)/2 diagonals. n(n − 3) = 70 = 10 × 7 gives n = 10. Check: C(10, 2) − 10 = 45 − 10 = 35.

q: Hina has 6 different fruits. In how many ways can she choose one or more of them?
x: Each fruit is either taken or not: 2⁶ = 64 subsets, i.e. C(6, 0) + C(6, 1) + … + C(6, 6) = 64. Removing the empty choice leaves 63. 720 = 6! counts orders, which do not matter here.

q: A committee of 5 is chosen from 6 men and 4 women. Usman (one of the men) must be on it and Hina (one of the women) must not. In how many ways can it be chosen?
x: Put Usman in and remove Hina: 4 more members come from the other 5 men and 3 women, so C(8, 4) = 70. 126 = C(9, 4) forgets to exclude Hina, and 56 = C(8, 5) forgets that Usman already fills one place.

q: An exam has 7 questions. A student must answer 5 of them, including at least 2 of the first 3. In how many ways can she choose her questions?
x: Either 2 of the first 3 and 3 of the last 4: C(3, 2) × C(4, 3) = 3 × 4 = 12, or all 3 of the first 3 and 2 of the last 4: 1 × C(4, 2) = 6. Total 12 + 6 = 18. 21 = C(7, 5) ignores the condition.

q: What is the value of C(12, 10)?
x: C(12, 10) = C(12, 2) = 12 × 11/2 = 66. 132 = P(12, 2) forgets to divide by 2!, and 2 confuses C(12, 10) with 12 − 10.

q: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a king or a heart?
x: P(king) + P(heart) − P(king of hearts) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. 17/52 counts the king of hearts twice; 1/52 is the probability of a card that is both a king and a heart.

q: A bag has 5 red and 3 white balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
x: P = (5/8) × (4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14. Equally, C(5, 2)/C(8, 2) = 10/28 = 5/14. 25/64 treats the draws as with replacement, and 15/28 is the probability of one ball of each colour.

q: Ali and Bilal try a problem independently. Ali solves it with probability 1/3 and Bilal with probability 1/4. What is the probability that exactly one of them solves it?
x: P(Ali only) + P(Bilal only) = (1/3)(3/4) + (2/3)(1/4) = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12. 7/12 = 1/3 + 1/4 ignores the other person failing, and 1/12 is the probability that both solve it.

q: E and F are mutually exclusive events with P(E) = 0.3 and P(F) = 0.45. What is the probability that neither E nor F happens?
x: Mutually exclusive means P(E ∩ F) = 0, so P(E ∪ F) = 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75 and P(neither) = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25. 0.385 = 1 − 0.75 + 0.135 wrongly treats the events as independent, and 0.135 = 0.3 × 0.45.

q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one of them shows a six?
x: P(no six) = (5/6)(5/6) = 25/36, so P(at least one six) = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36. Adding 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3 counts the double six twice, and 5/18 = 10/36 is exactly one six.
